The ISA allowance for 2026/27 is £20,000 per adult aged 18 or over. The tax year runs from 6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027.

You can split the £20,000 between cash, stocks and shares, and innovative finance ISAs, and a Lifetime ISA. The Lifetime ISA has its own limit of £4,000. Unused allowance does not carry forward.

You can pay up to £4,000 a year into a Lifetime ISA. That counts towards the £20,000 overall ISA allowance. The government adds a 25% bonus of up to £1,000 a year.

You must be aged 18 to 39 to open one. Withdrawals other than the permitted ones incur a 25% government charge. The permitted ones are buying a first home costing £450,000 or less after 12 months, withdrawals from age 60, and terminal illness. More detail is in the ISA guide: https://www.fernhillwealth.example/guides/isas/

Yes. A Lifetime ISA can be opened by anyone aged 18 to 39, so at 42 you can't open one.

You can still use the rest of the £20,000 yearly ISA allowance, for example in cash or stocks and shares ISAs. I can't advise on which would suit you. A qualified adviser can help with that if you'd like.

The ISA guide lists these changes from 6 April 2027:

- Investors under 65 can pay at most £12,000 a year into cash ISAs. The overall £20,000 allowance is unchanged, so the remainder can still go into stocks and shares or innovative finance ISAs. Investors aged 65 and over keep a £20,000 cash ISA limit.
- Transfers from stocks and shares or innovative finance ISAs into cash ISAs will no longer be permitted.
- A charge will apply to interest paid on cash held inside a stocks and shares or innovative finance ISA.
- Money already held in cash ISAs is not affected by the cap.

This is general information, not personal advice. Your adviser can discuss what it means for you. The guide is at https://www.fernhillwealth.example/guides/isas/

The £12,000 cash ISA cap applies from 6 April 2027 to investors under 65. You're 70, so it doesn't apply to you. Investors aged 65 and over keep a £20,000 cash ISA limit.
